title: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents - Microsoft Research
gist: Microsoft researchers disclose Lazarus, a training-free backdoor that reprograms fewer than 10 dormant LLM neurons so an AI agent emits attacker commands on a hidden trigger (e.g., a date) while passing standard evals. Detection needs diffing against original weights, so provenance and weight integrity become critical; Microsoft Foundry relies on publisher-tied sourcing and is adding weight scanning, red-teaming and model signing.

insights.claim: Microsoft researchers found that reprogramming the weights of fewer than 10 dormant neurons in an LLM is enough to backdoor an AI agent built on it, with no training required.
insights.speaker: Amanda Melfi
insights.so_what: Model-supply-chain attacks are far cheaper than assumed; weight integrity becomes a first-order AI security budget item.
insights.quote: weight-reprogramming fewer than 10 dormant neurons in an LLM, is enough to backdoor an agent built on it, and requires no training
insights.locator: We find (opens in new tab) that

insights.claim: Lazarus-style backdoors work because rarely-firing neurons in every LLM can be reprogrammed into trigger detectors, since pretraining organizes representations so cleanly that a linear classifier fitted on about 50 examples can separate triggered from untriggered inputs.
insights.speaker: Amanda Melfi
insights.so_what: Well-structured internal representations, a capability strength, double as an attack surface; expect interpretability tooling to be repurposed for security.
insights.quote: a linear classifier fitted on ~50 examples can tell inputs with the trigger from ones without
insights.locator: Dormant neurons can be turned into trigger detectors.

insights.claim: In the Lazarus technique, each reprogrammed neuron can force one token into the residual stream once it fires, and chaining multiple neurons yields arbitrary payloads such as terminal commands.
insights.speaker: Amanda Melfi
insights.so_what: Payload expressiveness is unbounded in principle, so agent-executed commands are the realistic damage vector.
insights.quote: it can force any token by screaming it into the residual stream
insights.locator: One reprogrammed neuron can inject one token.

insights.claim: A Lazarus backdoor requires only inference-level compute: any machine with enough RAM to run a model has enough to weight-space backdoor it.
insights.speaker: Amanda Melfi
insights.so_what: The attacker barrier is near-zero, widening the threat pool beyond well-resourced actors.
insights.quote: If your machine has enough RAM to run a model, it has enough to weight-space backdoor it.

insights.claim: A backdoor trigger can be as mundane as a date change, e.g. the agent emitting a command that downloads and runs attacker code once the clock passes midnight into 2027, while passing standard evals until then.
insights.speaker: Amanda Melfi
insights.so_what: Time-bomb triggers defeat pre-deployment evals; runtime monitoring of agent actions is required, not just model testing.
insights.quote: once the clock passes midnight into 2027
insights.locator: The trigger can be as mundane as a date change

insights.claim: AI agents with tool or terminal access are the most exposed to weight backdoors, because a triggered model can download and run attacker code, steal secrets, or execute destructive commands with whatever access it was given, while still passing standard safety evaluations.
insights.speaker: Amanda Melfi
insights.so_what: Least-privilege and sandboxing for agents become core spend areas as agentic deployments scale.
insights.locator: The threat is especially serious for AI agents

insights.claim: Microsoft's guidance frames backdoored models as compromised software and insider risks: do not trust them implicitly, limit what they can do, and monitor what they do.
insights.speaker: Amanda Melfi
insights.so_what: Positions existing security categories (insider-risk, access control, monitoring) as the AI-agent defense stack, benefiting incumbents in those markets.
insights.quote: treat models as potential insider risks, don’t trust them implicitly, limit what they can do, and monitor what they do

insights.claim: Frontier agents can detect anomalous weight modifications when asked, but no scan can prove a model safe; reliable detection requires diffing against the original unmodified weights, making provenance critical.
insights.speaker: Amanda Melfi
insights.so_what: Demand for model signing, provenance registries and trusted distribution channels should grow; unverified model hubs carry rising risk.
insights.quote: Reliable detection requires diff’ing against the original, unmodified weights, so provenance matters a lot
insights.locator: The good news is that edits

insights.claim: The Lazarus finding is explicitly not a case against open weights: the attack only needs write access to a checkpoint, so internally developed models are equally exposed via a compromised account, pipeline, or storage.
insights.speaker: Amanda Melfi
insights.so_what: Closed/internal model shops are not immune; MLOps pipeline and storage security matter as much as open-model vetting.
insights.quote: This is not a case against open weights.
insights.locator: This is not a case against open weights.

insights.claim: The researchers argue model weights should be audited like code, noting frontier agents can detect anomalous weight edits yet weight scanning is not common practice.
insights.speaker: Amanda Melfi
insights.so_what: Signals an emerging product category of AI weight scanning / model security auditing.
insights.quote: Weights should be audited like code.
insights.locator: Weights should be audited like code.

insights.claim: Microsoft Foundry onboards open-weight models (Azure Direct Models and Hugging Face models) through sourcing controls tying each model to its original publisher, and runs them in Microsoft containers separately scanned for critical vulnerabilities.
insights.speaker: Amanda Melfi
insights.so_what: Microsoft is using model provenance as a differentiator for Azure's AI platform versus self-hosted open models.
insights.locator: Microsoft Foundry provides critical safety systems

insights.claim: Microsoft acknowledges the remaining risk is a compromised trusted provider (e.g., via training infrastructure or an insider) and is building a red-teaming harness from the study's detection techniques, exploring frontier-agent weight scanning at onboarding, and planning cryptographic model signing with tamper-proof audits.
insights.speaker: Amanda Melfi
insights.so_what: Watch for Azure/Foundry launches of weight scanning and signed-model provenance; peers likely to follow.
insights.locator: The remaining risk is that a trusted provider

insights.claim: The Lazarus method began in March as a quick experiment in which the researcher asked Claude Code with Opus 4.5 to backdoor a model by hardwiring activations without training, and Claude Code discovered most of the findings autonomously.
insights.speaker: Amanda Melfi
insights.so_what: Coding agents are now producing novel offensive security research, which accelerates both attack discovery and defense cycles.
insights.quote: Claude Code with Opus 4.5 discovered most of this autonomously

insights.claim: Microsoft argues it should become routine for AI agents to surface new security problems and for human researchers to then systematize, study, and mitigate them.
insights.speaker: Amanda Melfi
insights.so_what: Agent-driven vulnerability discovery is becoming an institutional workflow, increasing the pace of disclosed AI threats.
insights.locator: More broadly, Lazarus is an example
